steps.title: Why joins are needed
steps.content: A join combines related rows from two tables using a matching condition. For example, Student.department_id can match Department.id.
steps.example: SELECT s.name, d.department_name FROM Student s JOIN Department d ON s.department_id = d.id;

steps.title: Choose an inner join
steps.prompt: Which join returns only rows with a match in both tables?
steps.explanation: INNER JOIN includes rows where the join condition matches on both sides.

steps.title: Left join keeps every left row
steps.content: LEFT JOIN returns all rows from the left table and matching rows from the right. If there is no match, right-side columns are NULL.
steps.example: Student LEFT JOIN Department keeps a student even if their department_id has no matching department.

steps.title: Understand unmatched rows
steps.prompt: A LEFT JOIN starts with Student and joins Department. A student has no matching department. What happens?
options: The student remains; Department columns are NULL
steps.explanation: LEFT JOIN preserves all left-table rows and fills unmatched right-side values with NULL.

steps.title: Join conditions matter
steps.content: Use ON to state how tables relate. A missing or incorrect join condition can create a Cartesian product or duplicate rows. FULL OUTER JOIN preserves unmatched rows from both sides when supported.
steps.tip: Before trusting a join, check whether the key is unique and whether one-to-many relationships are expected.

steps.title: Predict a SQL aggregate result
steps.content: A WHERE filter is applied before COUNT counts the remaining rows.
steps.prompt: What number does this query return?
steps.explanation: Two employee rows have department_id 10, so COUNT(*) returns 2.

steps.title: Write an INNER JOIN query
steps.content: Use the employee department_id to match the departments id. Return only employees who have a matching department.
steps.prompt: Write a query that returns each assigned employee's name and department name, ordered by employee id.
steps.sample_data:
employees
1 | Asha | 10 | 60000
2 | Ravi | 20 | 55000
3 | Mei | 10 | 65000
4 | Noor | NULL | 48000

departments
10 | Sales
20 | Engineering
steps.schema_ddl: CREATE TABLE employees (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL, department_id INTEGER, salary INTEGER); CREATE TABLE departments (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, department_name TEXT NOT NULL);
steps.seed_inserts: INSERT INTO employees VALUES (1, 'Asha', 10, 60000); INSERT INTO employees VALUES (2, 'Ravi', 20, 55000); INSERT INTO employees VALUES (3, 'Mei', 10, 65000); INSERT INTO employees VALUES (4, 'Noor', NULL, 48000); INSERT INTO departments VALUES (10, 'Sales'); INSERT INTO departments VALUES (20, 'Engineering');
steps.expected_query: SELECT e.name, d.department_name FROM employees AS e INNER JOIN departments AS d ON e.department_id = d.id ORDER BY e.id;
hints: Join employees to departments using employees.department_id = departments.id.
Use INNER JOIN so Noor is not included because her department_id is NULL. Finish with ORDER BY e.id.
steps.explanation: INNER JOIN keeps only employees with a matching department. Noor is excluded because NULL does not match a department id. ORDER BY e.id makes the output deterministic.

questions.prompt: Which join keeps all rows from the left table?
questions.explanation: LEFT JOIN preserves every left-table row.

questions.prompt: What is returned for an unmatched right-side row in a LEFT JOIN?
questions.explanation: Missing right-side values are represented as NULL.

questions.prompt: Which clause usually states the join-key relationship?
questions.explanation: ON specifies the matching condition for the join.

options: Only matching rows from both sides
questions.explanation: INNER JOIN returns pairs satisfying the join condition.

questions.prompt: Which join can return unmatched rows from both tables?
questions.explanation: FULL OUTER JOIN preserves matched and unmatched rows from both sides.
